tagline.text: A neo-Gothic Immaculate Conception shrine in Naic, Cavite, where a revolutionary assembly was held

location.label: Location
location.text: Captain Ciriaco Nazareno Street, Poblacion, Naic, Cavite

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–900 (Manila round-trip transport and snacks, per person)

children.text: Naic Church is the Immaculate Conception parish church and diocesan shrine in the town center of Naic, Cavite. Begun in the 19th century as a stone church, it stands out for its three-tier neo-Gothic facade and for being the site where Bonifacio held an assembly in 1897.

The official name of Naic Church is the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of the Immaculate Conception. It stands on Captain Ciriaco Nazareno Street in the Poblacion, the center of Naic, a town on Manila Bay in southwestern Cavite. Wikipedia gives the coordinates as roughly 14.32 degrees north and 120.76 degrees east, and several pilgrimage blogs give the same street address. It is about
44km
from Manila in a straight line and about
47km
by road.

From 1693 to 1768, Naic was a small mission outstation (visita) of the Church of Our Lady of the Assumption in Maragondon. It is said to have become an independent parish in 1796 with the Immaculate Conception as its patroness. Wikipedia-family sources also mention an official founding in 1627 and the purchase of the image as early as 1620, but the dates differ from source to source, so it is safest to check the on-site markers as well. The first church was a modest building of wood and cogon grass, and in 1835 Don Pedro Florentino began the stone church you see today, although some sources say it was built in 1839. For lack of funds, the bell tower was not finished until 1892.

In 1865 the Dominicans took over the parish and built a larger church and convent, said to be modeled on the Santo Domingo Church in Intramuros, Manila, which was lost in the war. The architecture is described as Earthquake Baroque, thickly built to withstand tremors, mixed with Gothic Revival. Before the war the church stood about five storeys tall and nearly ten blocks long, making it one of the largest and longest churches in Cavite, and in width it was second only to Imus Cathedral.

Its importance in Philippine history comes from what happened right after the Tejeros Convention on March 22, 1897. Andres Bonifacio made the church convent his headquarters, and the Naic Conference was held here. At this conference it is said that the old Tagalog letter on the flag was replaced with a Sun of Liberty with eight rays. A military agreement drawn up in Naic around the same time is also described as an attempt by Bonifacio to assert his authority against the Aguinaldo government. That makes the church a rewarding stop both for pilgrims and for travelers following the history of the revolution. According to Wikipedia, the church was restored in 2014 with support from the Wong Chu King Foundation, and local craftsmen under architect Noel Gatus later laid a classical-style mosaic floor in the central nave. On November 17, 1996, on the parish's 200th anniversary, Cardinal Ricardo Vidal dedicated the church, and on December 8 of that year it was declared a diocesan shrine. December 8 is still Naic's parish feast day and town fiesta.

The facade is divided into three levels, with a pointed-arch central entrance set between square pilasters. The pilasters rise to the triangular pediment and end in pinnacles, and a round window sits in the middle of the pediment. It is described as the only facade of its kind in Cavite, which makes it the best spot for photos.

blocks.title: Four-storey bell tower and cannon scar

children.text: On the left of the church stands a square four-storey bell tower with alternating round and pointed arched windows and a pyramidal roof. The crack in the tower is said to have been caused by a shell fired from Corregidor Island during World War II, and it has been deliberately preserved. Stand beneath the tower and look up to find the crack.

Inside, three major altars and two minor altars stand in the Gothic style. The main altar holds the image of the Immaculate Conception, the patroness of Naic. The statue is known as a full-figure wooden carving, and it is a lovely place to pause and pray.

blocks.title: Mosaic floor of the central nave

children.text: A classical-style mosaic floor laid during the restoration runs along the central aisle. The marble is said to have been supplied by Kaufman Stone. Because it is hard to walk through during Mass, visit quietly in the daytime when no Mass is being held.

This church grounds is where Bonifacio used the convent as his headquarters and held the Naic Conference. The convent building does not survive in its original form, so ask at the signboards or the parish office to get a sense of where it stood. Knowing the story of the rays on the Philippine flag makes the visit much more meaningful.

The Casa Hacienda de Naic, built by the religious order for administration, stands nearby and is now used by Naic Central School. Wikipedia describes it as the only friar-administered casa hacienda in the country still in use. Since it is a school facility, plan to view it from outside, and ask permission before going in.

blocks.title: December 8 feast of the Immaculate Conception

children.text: December 8 is both the parish feast day and the town fiesta of Naic. Around that date the area in front of the church is at its busiest, with Masses and processions and the liveliest atmosphere. Parking and traffic are crowded, so it is better to arrive early in the morning.

items.title: One-day history pilgrimage
items.subtitle: Naic Church and a stroll around the town

children.text: Leave from PITX or a southern terminal in Manila. Even on a weekday, roads toward Cavite can be congested, so an early start is best.
Arrive in downtown Naic and photograph the facade and bell tower from in front of the church. Look first for the crack in the tower and the round window in the facade.
Go inside and see the Immaculate Conception image on the main altar, the mosaic floor, and the five altars in turn. If people are praying, keep quiet and avoid flash.
Have lunch near the town market. The town has local eateries and street food stalls that are good for a simple meal.
If you want more revolutionary history, walk around the nearby Casa Hacienda and the town hall area. If time allows, continue to the churches in Maragondon or Tanza.
Head back to Manila before dark. Roads clog during the evening rush, so leaving around 4 p.m. is more comfortable.
Mass times differ by day, so check the parish Facebook page or local notices before you visit.
Start with the Holy Cross Church in Tanza. Naic and Tanza are described as about
apart.
Move on to Naic Church. According to a blog, the author drove about
from the church in Tanza, so travel time varies with traffic.
After lunch, go to the Church of the Assumption of Our Lady in Maragondon, about
from Naic.
On the way back, stop in Trece Martires for a rest and then head to Manila.
Chartering a vehicle or using a ride-hailing car such as Grab makes a route covering several churches in one trip much easier.
From Manila to Naic is about
47km
by road, around two hours without traffic and much longer in congestion.

From PITX (Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange), take a modern jeepney or bus toward Cavite to Tanza and transfer to a Naic jeepney. Alternatively, take a bus to Trece Martires and transfer to a Naic jeepney at SM Trece Martires.
The Naic jeepney from SM Trece Martires is reported to run from about 4 a.m. to about 9 p.m. (one listing says 24 hours), and the fare was about
as of January 2026. The March 2026 jeepney fare increase (traditional minimum ₱14, modern ₱17) may push it higher, so confirm locally.
Routes and fares from Manila change often, so check PITX information or the latest sources before you leave.
From Manila airport (MNL), combining a bus and a taxi to Naic is said to take around three hours.
If you have luggage or a group, going straight from the airport by Grab or taxi is easier. Fares vary greatly with traffic.
Take the expressway toward Cavite and come down through Trece Martires or Tanza to reach downtown Naic. The roads into town are narrow and can be congested.
The street in front of the church is narrow and parking may be limited, so look for parking near the market or town hall.
Downtown Naic can be explored on foot, and a tricycle costs a few tens of pesos depending on distance.
To reach nearby churches or the coast, use a tricycle or jeepney.

The church is open year-round and any time is fine, but December to May, with less rain, is the most comfortable for walking. In the heat of midday the strong sun makes the inside of the church feel pleasantly cool.

The December 8 feast of the Immaculate Conception brings Masses and processions that give you a feel for the town, but it is very crowded, so go early. During Holy Week, many people make a visita iglesia circuit of Cavite churches.

rows: Busiest, coinciding with the parish feast day (December 8)
Holy Week pilgrimage season; avoid midday and visit in the morning
Typhoons are common, so bring an umbrella and keep your schedule loose

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Downtown Naic does not have many large hotels, so most visitors make it a day trip. If you need to stay overnight, nearby Trece Martires or the Cavite coast offers more choices of lodging.

You can eat at the Naic public market and at eateries and street stalls in town. Try simple Cavite-style Filipino meals, and buy fruit and snacks at the market. Shop hours vary, so check on Sundays and holidays.
A church is a place of worship, so modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is best. During Mass, avoid taking photos and moving around.
Mass times vary by day and season, so check the parish Facebook page (Diocesan Shrine and Parish of Immaculate Conception Naic) or local notices.
To fit the whole facade in one shot, shoot wide-angle from across the road. Look up at the crack in the tower from up close.
The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat and water and visit in the morning.
If you are covering Cavite churches in one go, combining Tanza, Naic and Maragondon makes travel efficient.
Roads are very congested on the December 8 feast day, so use public transport and set out early.
Carry small cash. Many tricycles and market eateries do not take cards.
A church is a living place of faith, so be careful about visiting and photographing during Mass, and because dates and facts differ among sources, put the on-site information first.
Interior viewing may be restricted during Masses and events, so check parish news before you visit.
This area has heavy traffic, so allow generous travel time and check the last departure back to Manila in advance.
Watch out for pickpockets and phone theft, and keep valuables close to your body.
Dates for the church's construction (1835, 1839 and so on) and its founding (1627, 1796) differ among sources, so it is best not to pin them down to a single answer.
During typhoons and the rainy season, roads may flood, so check the latest weather information.

blocks.title: Church of the Assumption of Our Lady, Maragondon

children.text: This church in Maragondon, about
from Naic, was the parish to which Naic once belonged as a mission outstation. It fits well into a Cavite church pilgrimage route.
This church in Tanza is about
from Naic. It is a common stop on pilgrimage itineraries just before Naic Church.
Imus, the provincial capital of Cavite, is about
24km
from Naic and has Imus Cathedral. It is also interesting that before the war Naic Church was second in width only to Imus Cathedral.
This is the island said to have fired the shell that cracked Naic's bell tower. It is a war heritage site at the entrance of Manila Bay, best visited separately as a day trip.
